The off-design code was originally developed by James Crouse while he was an employee of NASA.
The code assumes steady, axisymmetric, two-dimensional flow in the meridional plane and uses a streamline curvature method for the aerodynamic solution.
The accuracy of the off-design performance predictions depends on the validity of the empirical flow loss and deviation correlation models.
The code can handle bleed flows and allows for the first five stators to be reset for each rotational speed.
The user example case is for a low-aspect-ratio two-stage fan, which is the same case used for the compressor design code.
The off-design code predictions are generally in good agreement with experimental data, especially for the 70% speed case.
The code can calculate speedlines greater than 100% of the design speed fraction.
The code is written in Fortran and can be obtained from COSMIC with the program number LEW-16176.
The off-design code was developed to be used in tandem with the compressor design code, with the design code providing the necessary blade geometry input.
The input data includes general parameters (e.g., number of speeds, choke/stall ranges) and detailed calculation station and blade row information.
The aerodynamic flow solution uses an inner and outer iteration scheme to solve the continuity and radial equilibrium equations.
The code includes empirical correlations for the profile loss coefficient and deviation angle, which are key factors in the off-design performance predictions.
For highly-loaded, large multistage compressors, the loss and deviation correlations may need improvement to better match experimental data.
The off-design code can compute through small reverse flow regions using the empirical loss and deviation models.
The controlling main routine in the code calculates reduced flow rates and rotational speeds for each desired speed fraction.
